steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a short paper presenting a library of commonsense ontology micropatterns built with help from an LLM, motivated by analogy and transfer learning and modular ontology modeling, and ending with the paper's outline.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Humans do transfer learning by making analogous connections, so they understand the unknowns of the world using knowledge they acquired before. When solving problems, humans find similarities between their current problem and earlier ones and draw logical connections that may help them find a working solution. Whether it works or not, this then becomes part of the learning process for the next round of problem-solving. To draw similarities, humans have to use their logical skills to generalize a problem or concept so they can adapt it from what they already know.

Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are pursuing General AI, and they also want this ability to do transfer and analogy learning. We think that using modular ontology is one way to do this. The idea is to start with a simple and (perhaps) well-understood pattern of knowledge and adapt it to new scenarios and use-cases, and we call the mechanism for doing this modularization. The overall methodology is called Modular Ontology Modeling (MOMo), and by now it is an established paradigm for building knowledge graphs (KG) and their schemas, i.e., an ontology.

ODPs and MODLs:
- ontology design patterns = tiny ontologies for domain-invariant modeling problems; usual starting point for MOMo
- from Ontology Design Pattern Portal or MODLs
- MODLs: annotated, curated collections of ODPs + queryable index ontology

This paper:
- CS-MODL: library of commonsense micropatterns
- commonsense = “what first comes to mind”; LLM asked about common properties of common nouns
- micropatterns: no rich semantics; rdfs:domain and rdfs:range, no complicated OWL axioms
- methodology for 104 micropatterns, example, online resource

Organization: Section 2 methodology, Section 3 example, Section 4 contributions, Section 5 future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Humans do transfer learning by making analogous connections, so they understand the unknowns of the world using knowledge they acquired before. When solving problems, humans find similarities between their current problem and earlier ones and draw logical connections that may help them find a working solution. Whether it works or not, this then becomes part of the learning process for the next round of problem-solving. To draw similarities, humans have to use their logical skills to generalize a problem or concept so they can adapt it from what they already know.

Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are pursuing General AI, and they also want this ability to do transfer and analogy learning. We think that using modular ontology is one way to do this. The idea is to start with a simple and (perhaps) well-understood pattern of knowledge and adapt it to new scenarios and use-cases, and we call the mechanism for doing this modularization. The overall methodology is called Modular Ontology Modeling (MOMo), and by now it is an established paradigm for building knowledge graphs (KG) and their schemas, i.e., an ontology.

The usual starting point for the MOMo methodology is ontology design patterns, which are tiny ontologies meant to solve domain-invariant modeling problems. They can come from many places, including the Ontology Design Pattern Portal or Modular Ontology Design Libraries (MODLs). MODLs are annotated, curated collections of ODPs, together with an index ontology that can be queried for patterns of different types and for relationships between patterns.

In this paper we provide such a design library, called CS-MODL, which is made of commonsense micropatterns. For this work, we define the words in our title.

- By commonsense we loosely mean “what first comes to mind.” Here we ask an LLM about common properties of common nouns (see below) and get some simple and naïve responses, which are then encoded into:

- micropatterns, which we contrast with ODPs. Here micropatterns do not have sophisticated or rich semantics. They are defined using rdfs:domain and rdfs:range, without more complicated OWL axioms.

Concretely, we describe the methodology we used to build the 104 commonsense micropatterns in CS-MODL, discuss an example, and provide the library as an online resource.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces our methods for getting the right information from the LLM we chose and for building the commonsense micropatterns. Section 3 gives an example of a generated commonsense micropattern. Section 4 summarizes the contributions of our commonsense pattern library. Section 5 ends the paper with notes on future areas that we see as next steps for this research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Humans perform transfer learning through analogous connections, understanding the unknowns of the world with previously acquired knowledge [1,2]. In problem-solving, humans find similarities in their current problem to draw logical connections that may help in finding a working solution, which, regardless of success, becomes part of the learning process for the next iteration of problem-solving. Drawing similarities requires humans to use their logical skills to generalize a problem or concept so that it can be adapted from their acquired knowledge.

Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, in their pursuit of General AI, also seek this ability to conduct transfer and analogy learning. We posit that the use of modular ontology is one way this can be accomplished [3]. In particular, the notion of starting with a simple and (perhaps) well-understood pattern of knowledge and adapting it to new scenarios and use-cases; we call the mechanism by which we accomplish this modularization. This overarching methodology is known as Modular Ontology Modeling (MOMo), and it is by now an established paradigm for constructing knowledge graphs (KG) and their schemas (i.e., an ontology) [4].

Ontology design patterns, tiny ontologies intended to solve domain-invariant modeling problems [5], are the usual starting point for the MOMo methodology. They may be sourced from many places, including the Ontology Design Pattern Portal or Modular Ontology Design Libraries (MODLs) [6]. MODLs are annotated, curated collections of ODPs, combined with an index ontology that can be queried for patterns of different types and for relationships between patterns.

In this paper, we provide such a design library, which we call CS-MODL, composed of commonsense micropatterns. For the purposes of this work, we define our title.

- By commonsense we loosely mean “what first comes to mind.” In this case, we ask an LLM about common properties of common nouns (as discussed below) and receive some simple and naïve responses, which are then encoded into:

- micropatterns, which we contrast with ODPs. In this case, micropatterns do not have sophisticated or rich semantics. Indeed, they are defined using rdfs:domain and rdfs:range, without more complicated OWL axioms.

Concretely, we describe the methodology we used to construct the 104 commonsense micropatterns contained in CS-MODL, discuss an example, and provide the library as an online resource.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces our methodologies for obtaining the appropriate information from our chosen LLM and for constructing the commonsense micropatterns. Section 3 provides an example of a generated commonsense micropattern. Section 4 summarizes the contributions of our commonsense pattern library. Section 5 concludes the paper with notes on future areas we see as next steps for this research.
